title: Dog and Cat Protection Act
raw_text:
With some simple changes to state law, Pennsylvania can do a much better job at protecting animals being bred and used for research in animal testing laboratories, and from kennels and dealers who face serious or multiple citations under the Dog and Cat Protection Act.
The bill, introduced in the Senate by state Senators Carolyn Comitta and Doug Mastriano would restrict the import and sale of animals (not just beagles) from kennels and dealers with serious or multiple citations under the federal Animal Welfare Act, require those breeding dogs and cats for medical or scientific experimentation to keep records, enhance animal adoption, and close loopholes in our animal cruelty law.
SB 381: The Beagle Bill
Prevents laboratories from using state funds to support painful experiments on dogs and cats.
Blocks public funds from being used to devocalize dogs or cats in laboratories or to purchase dogs or cats who have been devocalized.
Prevents dealers and kennels from selling or attempting to sell dogs and cats born at facilities with serious or sustained Animal Welfare Act citations.
Requires laboratories to allow dogs and cats the chance to be adopted into loving homes after the experiments are over.
Mandates that institutions receiving state funding disclose information about animal experiments conducted at their facilities and the amount of the state funding used for animal experiments.
Requires laboratories that test pesticides, drugs, cosmetics, chemicals or other products on animals to use nonanimal tests once approved by the proper regulatory agencies.

ai_summary.summary: State Senators Carolyn Comitta and Doug Mastriano introduced Senate Bill 381, known as the Beagle Bill, which would restrict the use of state funds for painful animal experiments, require laboratories to offer animals for adoption after experiments end, block purchases of animals from facilities with serious federal Animal Welfare Act violations, and mandate a transition to non-animal testing methods once alternatives are approved by regulators. The bill also requires state-funded institutions to publicly disclose their animal testing activities and associated spending.

title: LGBTQ – Bills We Are Proud Of
raw_text:
Bills We Are Proud Of
Senator Carolyn T. Comitta is a champion of LGBTQ+ equality and rights for the benefit of all communities, individuals and families across Pennsylvania.
As a member of West Chester Borough Council in 2006, she helped lead the effort to make West Chester the first municipality in Chester County — and among the first in the Commonwealth — to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, housing, and public accommodations.
Later, during her tenure as Mayor of West Chester, Comitta celebrated the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark ruling in
Obergefell v. Hodges
and presided over numerous weddings of loving same-sex couples.
In the state senate, Comitta serves on the LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus and continues to be a strong supporter and vocal advocate for legislation to ensure that all LGBTQ+ Pennsylvanians are treated with respect, fairness, and equal rights under the law. That includes measures to protect LGBTQ+ students from discrimination, updating our laws to reflect the rights of same-sex couples to marry, and more.
My LGBTQ+ Legislation
^
SB 434
(Sen. Comitta)
While the landmark U.S. Supreme Court ruling Obergefell v. Hodges made marriage equality the law of the land, outdated laws still remain on the books in Pennsylvania that define marriage as only being between a man and a woman. It is a disservice to all our fellow Pennsylvanians in loving, same-sex marriages to continue to allow this obsolete section of law to exist. This legislation will remove the prohibition of same sex marriage and affirm Pennsylvania’s commitment to equality for all.
^
Bill # Pending
(Sen. Comitta)
Prohibits a service provider form denying any person the opportunity to become an adoptive or foster parent or delaying or denying the placement of a child based on the real or perceived disability, race, creed, religion, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, national origin, ancestry, or any communicable disease, including HIV. For the sake of the children waiting to be adopted and our friends and neighbors in the LGBTQ community, nondiscrimination laws are needed to protect the rights of families and allow more children the chance to find a permanent and loving home.
^
SB 496
(Sen. Comitta and Sen. L. Williams)
Educational Improvement and Opportunity Scholarship Tax Credits (EITC & OSTC) provide scholarships that help Pennsylvania children afford a school other than their school district of residence. Unfortunately, LGBTQ+ students are frequently denied support by some private schools that choose to discriminate against them in the admissions process. This is completely unacceptable. I’ve partnered with Senator Lindsey Williams to introduce legislation to protect these students by requiring schools that receive funding through these programs to have a written policy of nondiscrimination.
Removing Administrative Barriers
^
SB 189
(Sen. Street)
Collects demographic data with the inclusion of a voluntary LGBTQ+ identifier question on state forms to gather critical data needed to combat anti-LGBTQ+ efforts and better serve LGBTQ+ individuals in the community.
^
SB 448
(Sen. Cappelletti)
Creates a new administrative name change process that is simpler and streamlined.
^
SB 521
(Sen. Muth)
Makes the publication requirements more affordable and creates privacy protections. Eliminates the publication requirement and make automatic sealing of records the default.
^
SB 437
(Sen. L. Williams)
Reduces the delays, cost, and confusion involved in the current name change process by requiring publicly available information on name change process, dedicated safe point of contact, and training.
^
SB 510
(Sen. Kearney)
Removes legal barriers and creates Name Change Assistance Grants for Transgender Pennsylvanians.
Economic Justice
^
SB 389
(Sen. Boscola)
Prohibits the denial of credit based on sexual orientation, gender identity, or expression.
^
Bill # Pending
(Sen. Street)
Designates $2.5 million from the Lottery Fund to support a LGBTQ Senior Community Grant Program.
^
Bill # Pending
(Sen. Muth)
Requires insurance coverage for the expenses of any post-exposure prophylaxis HIV medication.
^
Bill # Pending
(Sen. Muth)
Requires insurance coverage for pre-exposure prophylaxis HIV medication.
Hate Crime Prevention
^
SB 212
(Sen. Collett)
Prohibits the criminal justice loophole of the “Gay and trans panic” homicide defense
^
Bill # Pending
(Sen. Boscola)
Expands the legal definition of ethnic intimidation to include and add the same protections for hate-based intimidation based on ancestry, sex, gender or gender identity, sexual orientation, intellectual disability, physical or sensory disability or behavioral or mental health.
^
Bill # Pending
(Sen. Costa)
Helps prevent hate crimes by including penalties for intimidation and a reporting system for schools and post-secondary instuitions that would allow for better protection of our LGBTQ+ community
Social Justice
^
SB 388
(Sen. Boscola)
A Constitutional amendment to prohibit discrimination based on an individual’s sexual orientation, gender identity, or expression.
^
Bill # Pending
(Sen. Santarsiero and Sen. Saval)
Adds sexual orientation, gender identity, or expression to the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act.

The page also highlights related bills introduced by other senators covering name change processes, hate crime laws, insurance coverage, and civil rights protections.

title: Comitta, Williams Announce Funding for More Improvements at Ash Park

Comitta, Williams Announce Funding for More Improvements at Ash Park
October 7, 2026
West Chester, Pa. (October 7, 2026)
– Plans to continue improving and developing Coatesville’s largest and most visited park got a major boost today thanks to state funding announced by State Senator Carolyn Comitta and State Representative Dan Williams.
Phase three of the Ash Park development plan was awarded $900,000 in funding through the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR) Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2).
“The new Ash Park is a center of the Coatesville community where children, families, and residents can come to gather, play, cool off, get some exercise, or just enjoy the fresh air and sunshine. This investment will help the city and its partners continue to develop the site, creating more opportunity for safe, healthy outdoor recreation for the entire community,” Comitta said.
“This funding is an investment in the quality of life and long-term vitality of communities in the 74th District. Enhancing parks and recreational opportunities benefit residents in multiple meaningful ways. I’m proud to advocate for these investments and help bring these improvements to our communities,” Rep. Williams said.
Earlier this year, Ash Park reopened with new features, including three renovated basketball courts, a pavilion with a seating area and restrooms, an expanded play and recreation area, upgraded horseshoe pits, and a new splash pad. Those improvements represented the first two phases of a
multi-phase master plan
for the 9.3-acre park. Forthcoming phases call for a new soccer field, new playground equipment, and an additional picnic pavilion at Ash Park.
The C2P2 grant program is funded by a variety of state and federal funding sources. The Ash Park project was funded through the Land and Water Conservation Fund.

title: Comitta Announces State Funding for Sports Courts at Exton Park
raw_text:
Comitta Announces State Funding for Sports Courts at Exton Park
October 7, 2026
West Chester, Pa. (October 7, 2026)
– New courts for tennis, pickleball, and basketball are coming to Exton Park, thanks to funding announced today by State Senator Carolyn Comitta.
The project is funded through the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR) Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2).
“Exton Park is an important community asset that brings together opportunities for outdoor recreation, organized sports, miles of hiking and walking loops, links regional trails, playing areas for young children, a dog park, and soon, new tennis, pickleball, and basketball courts,” Comitta said. “The park serves tens of thousands of residents in West Whiteland and nearby municipalities. As we see development continue to impact the area, it’s important that we continue to invest in Exton Park as a place for families and children to relax, enjoy the outdoors, get active, and connect with neighbors.”
Exton Park is a 727-acre property jointly owned by West Whiteland Township and Chester County, which acquired it from the Church Farm School more than three decades ago.
Since then, the park has embarked on a masterplan that has included opening of three public multi-use fields, a trailhead for the Chester Valley Trail with modern restroom facilities, the Pennypacker trailhead, picnic pavilions, and more. In addition, the park’s Swedesford Recreation Area features a large playground and zipline, a tot lot, a dog park, a disc golf course, benches, restrooms, water fountains, and parking.
The new sports courts and additional parking area are part of Phase III of the development of the park.
The C2P2 grant program is funded by a variety of state and federal funding sources. The Exton Park project was funded through the Land and Water Conservation Fund.

title: Comitta, Shusterman Announce Funding for an Addition to the Rushton Woods Preserve

Comitta, Shusterman Announce Funding for an Addition to the Rushton Woods Preserve
October 7, 2026
West Chester, Pa. (October 7, 2026)
– State Senator Carolyn Comitta and State Representative Melissa Shusterman announced today that funding was awarded for an addition to the Rushton Woods Preserve in Willistown.
The Willistown Conservation Trust (WCT) was awarded $1.5 million in state funding for the project through the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2).
The funds will support the acquisition of land to add to the Ruston Woods Preserve, an 86-acre preserve managed by WCT.
“As development pressures continue to close in on our region, investments in open space and forest preservation are increasingly important. The Rushton Woods Preserve is a place where families can go to experience nature, get active, enjoy the outdoors, and learn about the importance of local wildlife and ecology,” Comitta said. “I want to thank DCNR, and the Willistown Conservation Trust for working together to expand this environmental treasure.”
“Rushton Woods plays an important role in our communities: it supports environmental health, protects our natural resources, and provides a space for our residents to connect with each other and nature. I’m grateful to the DCNR for recognizing the importance of preservation and conservation of these spaces in our communities and all across the Commonwealth,” said Shusterman.
The preserve currently features three miles of pedestrian and equestrian trails, a 1,200-foot-long segment of Okehocking Run, meadows, wetlands, and mature woodland, an important bird area and federally licensed bird banding station, and more than 150 shrubs and native species. It’s also home to the Ruston Community Farm and Rushton Conservation Center, which host a variety of WCT community and educational events.
The C2P2 grant program is funded by a variety of state and federal funding sources. The Rushton Woods project was funded through the Keystone Fund.

Comitta, Pielli Announce Funding for Parks in West Chester and East Bradford
October 7, 2026
West Chester, Pa. (October 7, 2026) – Two parks in East Bradford Township and West Chester Borough are slated for major upgrades thanks to state funding announced today by State Senator Carolyn Comitta and State Representative Chris Pielli.
The projects are funded through the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR) Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2).
John O. Green Park in West Chester was awarded $250,000 to replace aging playground equipment, install compliant safety surfaces and fall zones, extend the pavilion to expand usable shade and gathering space, add green/natural play areas, and make targeted site and safety upgrades. The improvements aim to ensure that the park remains an inclusive, engaging play environment for children of all abilities.
East Bradford Park was awarded $900,000 to replace outdated playgrounds with new, fully inclusive play equipment, add poured-in-place safety surfacing, replace the aging tennis and pickleball courts, add a new tennis ball wall, replace the aging baseball scoreboard, redesign and retrofit the existing parking lot and pedestrian access, add new accessible drinking fountains, install native landscaping, and add shaded areas near play areas. The upgrades are designed to enhance the park’s usability, sustainability, and long-term value to the community.
“Parks, trails, playgrounds, and playing fields and courts are a big part of the strong quality of life in communities across Chester County. With these investments, we are expanding options for children, families, and visitors to get some exercise, enjoy the outdoors, meet up with friends and neighbors, and more,” said Comitta. “I want to thank Rep. Pielli and our partners in East Bradford and West Chester for their work in continuing to promote health and well-being through outdoor recreation and activity.”
“At a time when land availability is shrinking, investing in our current parks and green spaces is extremely crucial,” Pielli said. “These grants to East Bradford Township and West Chester Borough will help them continue to protect, preserve, and improve our shared land now and for future generations. My team and I are proud to work with State Senator Comitta and her staff to identify, support, and advocate for District grants through every step of the process, so that every resident can reap the benefits of this DCNR funding. I look forward to visiting these parks to see these improvements take shape in our community!”
Named after a former West Chester Chief of Police, John O. Green Park was developed, with state support, on a remediated site nearly two decades ago. The park serves an area of the borough where families may face greater barriers to accessing safe, high-quality recreation. The proposed improvements will help address those gaps and align with the borough’s plans to support equitable public health, youth development, and neighborhood well-being in underserved areas. In addition, the borough is already undertaking a significant park update by investing in improvements to its splashpad, including new water play features and an enhanced fall zone designed for easier long-term maintenance.
East Bradford Park plays a vital role in the community, featuring the only non-school-owned public playground and public tennis and pickleball courts in the township.
The C2P2 grant program is funded by a variety of state and federal funding sources. The West Chester and East Bradford projects were funded through the Land and Water Conservation Fund and the Keystone Fund.

title: Comitta, Shusterman Announce Funding for the Tredyffrin Heritage Center at Duportail
raw_text:
Comitta, Shusterman Announce Funding for the Tredyffrin Heritage Center at Duportail
September 18, 2026
West Chester, Pa. (September 15, 2026)
– A historic site in Tredyffrin that played an important role in the Revolutionary War is becoming a heritage and visitors’ center to support tourism and share the story of American Independence.
This week, state Senator Carolyn Comitta and state Representative. Melissa Shusterman announced that the Commonwealth Finance Authority awarded state funding for accessibility upgrades at the 18th-century Duportail House and Federal Barn.
“As we come off the 250th anniversary of our nation, it’s important that we continue to preserve the landmarks and share the stories surrounding our region’s leading role in the fight for freedom and independence,” Comitta said. “I hope this investment will open the history of the Duportail House up to even more visitors and families who come to learn and experience all that Tredyffrin and Chester County have to offer.”
The investment will support transforming the site into an ADA-accessible, visitor-ready heritage destination. In addition to making ADA-compliant upgrades to an existing restroom and ramp construction, the project calls for new signage and structural modifications in preparation for new exhibits and enhanced visitor amenities.
During the Continental Army’s encampment at Valley Forge in 1777-78, the Duportail House served as headquarters for General Louis Lebègue Duportail, a French military engineer, who was George Washington’s Chief Engineer of the Continental Army.
Recruited by Benjamin Franklin and loaned by France, Duportail  planned Valley Forge’s defenses during the Revolutionary War’s darkest hours, designing fortifications that could enable Washington’s troops to hold off a potential attack by the British army, which was encamped in nearby Philadelphia.
While those defenses were never tested, Duportail went on to help establish the U.S. Military Academy at West Point and is credited with founding what would become the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. His motto “Essayons” (“Let us try”) remains the Corps’ official motto today.
Comitta worked with State Rep. Melissa Shusterman to help secure the $25,000 grant through the Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development’s Local Share Account Program.
“I’m proud to have been able to bring money back to my district,” Shusterman said. “We’re thankful to live in a Commonwealth that continues to invest in our communities. Whether it’s urgent infrastructure needs, upgraded equipment for our first responders or new innovations for county tourism, our economy works for the people who work hard to contribute to it.”
The initiative also aligns with local heritage tourism and economic development strategies, aiming to boost public engagement and regional tourism.
Today, the Duportail House and barn have been restored and serve as a wedding venue and event space. Both structures are also listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Chester County aims to mitigate flood hazards by expanding detection capabilities, implementing flood hazard signage on roadways, and installing traffic safety barriers during floods. The project calls for installing five flood sensors at high-risk streams, roadway closure gates at eight locations, and flood risk signage at twenty-seven locations.

As students begin to return to schools around our region, state Senator Carolyn Comitta is reminding motorists to follow Pennsylvania’s School Bus Stopping Law and to slow down to 15 mph in school zones.
Over the past five years, 8,302 citations were issued to Pennsylvania drivers for illegally passing a school bus, and 16,834 were issued for speeding in a school zone, according to data released from the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts. Drivers in Chester County accounted for about 6 percent of those citations.
“The fall back-to-school season is a busy time of year, especially for families with children. “There are more school buses on the road, more kids at bus stops, and an increase in traffic, as some drivers begin new commutes and routines,” said Comitta, a former public-school teacher and member of the Senate Education Committee. “Please slow down, stay focused, allow extra time for travel, and be sure to stop when you see a school bus with red lights flashing and stop arms extended.”
Under
Pennsylvania’s School Bus Stopping Law
:
Motorists must stop at least 10 feet away from school buses that have their red lights flashing and stop arms extended.
Motorists must stop when they are behind a bus, overtaking a bus, meeting a bus, or approaching an intersection where a bus is stopped.
Motorists following or traveling alongside a school bus must also stop until the red lights have stopped flashing, the stop arm is withdrawn, and all children have reached safety.
If physical barriers such as grassy medians, guide rails, or concrete median barriers separate oncoming traffic from the bus, motorists in the opposing lanes may proceed without stopping.
Do not proceed until all the children have reached a place of safety.
The penalties for violating the School Bus Stopping Law can be significant, including a 60-day driver’s license suspension, five points on your driving record, and a $250 fine.
Motorists are also reminded to slow down to the posted speed limit of 15 mph in school zones, which are particularly busy in the morning and afternoon hours during student arrival and dismissal.
In addition, this summer, full enforcement began of a new state law prohibiting the use of a handheld device while driving. Under the new law, which is a primary offense, drivers cannot talk on a handheld phone, text, record video, take pictures, play games, send emails, or use social media. The penalty is a $50 fine, plus court costs and other fees. Hands-free options like Bluetooth or CarPlay are permitted.

Op/Ed: Beagles are the All-American Dog, Pa Can Do Better to Protect Them (and Other Dogs and Cats, too)
August 13, 2026
When most of us think of beagles, we think of Snoopy and Charlie Brown. In addition to cementing their place in popular culture, beagles are ideal companions due to their gentle nature, and sturdy yet compact size.
Unfortunately, those same characteristics make them a choice breed for laboratory testing. All too often, many of these tests are painful, do not provide information relevant to humans, and end in euthanasia whether or not the dogs are fit for adoption. Worse yet, sometimes taxpayers are funding these inhumane tests, and they don’t even know it.
In Pennsylvania, we’re working to change that.
I’ve partnered with State Senator Doug Mastriano to introduce
Senate Bill 381
. While it’s affectionately known as “the Beagle Bill,” the bipartisan legislation protects all dogs (and cats) from cruelty by ending the sale of animal-tested cosmetics in the Commonwealth, and ensuring healthy pets have a chance for adoption after the experiments are over. It also calls for increasing transparency in animal experiments and blocking the use of state taxpayer dollars to fund experiments that cause pain or distress without relief.
The bill was passed by the Pennsylvania Senate unanimously in the fall but has been tied up in the House Judiciary Committee since then. We need to get it passed in the House and onto the governor’s desk before the legislative session ends this year, or we’ll be forced to restart the process in 2027.
In addition to our love of pets, the Beagle Bill was inspired by the rescue of roughly 4,000 beagles from Envigo, a facility in Virginia that bred dogs to be sold to laboratories for animal experimentation. Four years ago this summer, federal authorities raided Envigo after investigations revealed horrific violations of the Animal Welfare Act.
Fortunately, many of these dogs were adopted into loving homes, including dozens right here in Pennsylvania. Snoopy can’t speak for himself, but these real-life pups and their adopters have become powerful advocates for change, attending rallies, lobbying lawmakers in Harrisburg, and even getting together for annual reunions around the state. And their work is making a difference. A
June 2026 poll by Remington Research Group
revealed that 80% of registered voters supported the Beagle Bill, with only 5% opposed.
But the Beagle Bill isn’t just popular with voters; it’s sound policy that is backed by science. Animal tests are often poor predictors of human safety. In fact, more than 90% of drugs safe for animals fail in humans. Alternative methods based on human biology are much more likely to provide accurate results while also saving time and reducing costs. That’s why the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the National Institutes of Health, and the Environmental Protection Agency are all moving away from animal testing in favor of advanced human-relevant methods and models.
Furthermore, a growing number of states and industry leaders in cosmetics, personal care, and pharmaceuticals are already phasing out animal testing. The Beagle Bill would make Pennsylvania the
13
th
state to end the sale of cosmetics
produced with animal testing, and it aligns with the cosmetics industry itself
endorsing a similar federal ban
. Similarly,
seventeen other states
have passed comparable laws requiring healthy research dogs be released for adoption when they are retired from research purposes.
Over the last 15 years, Pennsylvania has made major strides in cracking down on puppy mills and advancing humane standards. Still, the growing consensus is we can do better. The Beagle Bill is an important part of that movement – sending the message that dogs belong on laps, not in labs. We can advance lifesaving treatments for people without inflicting unnecessary suffering on dogs and cats. We can accelerate the delivery of safer treatments to patients while reducing costs and saving thousands of laboratory animals each year.
The Beagle Bill will ensure that Pennsylvania does not become the site of the next Envigo. It will provide more than 2,100 dogs and 1,100 cats used in Pennsylvania laboratories with the chance to spend the rest of their lives in loving homes. It aligns with public opinion, ongoing federal efforts, and changes in major industries. It’s a win for ethics, innovation, bipartisanship, and animals.
Please call your state representative and tell them to vote for the Beagle Bill. If that isn’t enough to get it passed, in the words of Charlie Brown, “Good Grief!”
Carolyn Comitta, of West Chester, serves as State Senator for Pennsylvania’s 19
th
District. She is a sponsor of the Beagle Bill (Senate Bill 381) with Senator Doug
Mastriano in the Pennsylvania Senate.
NOTE:
This opinion piece appeared in PennLive under the title “Good grief! The PA House needs to pass the Beagle Bill now” on August 12, 2026.

title: Comitta: New Law Makes It Easier for Pa-Certified Teachers to Return to Commonwealth Classrooms

Comitta: New Law Makes It Easier for Pa-Certified Teachers to Return to Commonwealth Classrooms
July 29, 2026
Harrisburg, PA (July 28, 2026) –
A new law will make it easier for Pennsylvania teachers to return to the Commonwealth after teaching in other states.
As part of this year’s School Code, passed through the state budget process, the Pennsylvania Department of Education (PDE) will honor continuing education credits that are accepted by other states to maintain an active Pennsylvania teaching certificate.
The measure is based on
legislation introduced
by State Senator Carolyn Comitta to ease the pathway to Pennsylvania-certified teachers to rejoin the Commonwealth’s educator workforce should they leave, temporarily teach in another state, and then move back.
Comitta, a former public-school teacher, said she was inspired to introduce the legislation because teachers in military families or those who take longer-term, out-of-state teaching assignments previously faced losing their authorization to teach in Pennsylvania.
“As we continue to face a growing teacher shortage, this is another simple way we can cut through barriers and help get more talented and qualified teachers into Pennsylvania classrooms,” Comitta, who serves on the Senate Education Committee, said. “It will be especially beneficial to counties that border neighboring states, like Chester County, where West Chester University is a leader in producing Pennsylvania-certified teachers.”
By law, Pennsylvania educators must complete 180 hours of professional development, 6 college/collegiate credits, or 6 continuing professional education (CPE) credits every five years to keep their certification active.
If an educator fails to complete the requisite credits within the allotted time, their certificate is placed on “inactive status,” and they become unauthorized to teach in Pennsylvania.
Previously, the Pennsylvania Department of Education was unable to accept continuing education credits from other states, making it very difficult for Pennsylvania-certified educators to maintain an active teaching certification here.
Now, educators will not have to face the additional barrier of completing continuing education or academic credits if their certification becomes inactive while they are teaching outside the Commonwealth.

title: Comitta: Farmers Can Apply for Tax Credits to Improve Soil and Water Quality Beginning August 1

Comitta: Farmers Can Apply for Tax Credits to Improve Soil and Water Quality Beginning August 1
July 28, 2026
West Chester, PA (July 28, 2026) –
Beginning August 1, farmers, businesses, and landowners can apply for tax credits for equipment and projects that improve soil health and water quality, state Senator Carolyn Comitta announced.
Through the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture’s
Resource Enhancement & Protection (REAP) Program
, $13 million in total tax credits are available to help pay for farm enhancements that protect the environment and profitability, as well as their ability to pass a sustainable farm down to the next generation.
“Farmers work closely with our environment, and this program can help them lead the way in boosting innovation, conservation, and their bottom lines,” said Comitta, who serves on the Senate Agricultural and Rural Affairs Committee. “REAP has been a Pennsylvania success story in promoting investment in environmentally friendly upgrades that support clean water, healthy soil, and sustainable agriculture.”
REAP helps agricultural producers implement best management practices or purchase equipment to reduce nutrient and sediment runoff, enhance soil health and improve water quality across the mid-Atlantic region. Eligible projects include purchasing no-till planting equipment or precision nutrient application equipment, constructing manure storage structures, planting cover crops or forested riparian buffers, establishing grazing practices, excluding livestock from streams, and more.
“More than ever, Pennsylvania farmers are investing their own resources in cleaner water and productive soil to sustain us in the future,” Pennsylvania Agriculture Secretary Russell Redding said. “Their dollars, multiplied by support from historic levels of investment under the Shapiro Administration
,
are paying off in the form of healthier waterways and a greener future for Pennsylvania farms and communities.”
REAP provides tax credits at 50%, 75%, or 90% of costs incurred for implementing BMPs that reduce nitrogen, phosphorus, and sediment pollution. Credits are issued after a practice is installed or eligible equipment is purchased.
REAP credits can also be combined with other state funding, including the
Agriculture Conservation Assistance Program
, and
Conservation Excellence Grants
, as well as federal funding.
Pennsylvania’s
State Conservation Commission
, a partnership of the Pennsylvania Departments of Agriculture and Environmental Protection, is accepting applications for REAP tax credits beginning August 1. In addition, through REAP’s sponsorship program, another business could help finance a project and apply for the tax credit instead of the producer.
REAP tax credits are awarded on a first-come, first-served basis until funds are exhausted. Baseline eligibility includes compliance with the PA Clean Streams Law and the Pennsylvania Nutrient and Odor Management Law.
Due to the program’s popularity, funds may run out before the October 31, 2026, application deadline.
Since REAP’s inception in 2007, Pennsylvania has awarded over $200 million in state income tax credits to farmers and businesses for more than 10,000 projects on approximately 4,000 farms.
Improvements from these projects have kept 8 million pounds of nitrogen, 500,000 pounds of phosphorus, and 400,000 tons of sediment out of Pennsylvania streams, rivers, and the waterways they feed.

title: Comitta Secures Investment in Historic Berwyn Church that Helped Fight School Segregation

Comitta Secures Investment in Historic Berwyn Church that Helped Fight School Segregation
July 22, 2026
Devon, PA (July 22, 2026) –
A historic Main Line church that played a key role in the Civil Rights movement and the fight against school segregation is getting some much-needed infrastructure upgrades, thanks to grant funding secured by State Senator Carolyn Comitta.
Mt. Zion African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church is receiving $50,000 in state funding to repair water damage to the historic structure, which was built in 1861. It is considered the first recorded and oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church on the entire Main Line. In the 1930s, the church served as an important meeting place for African American families and leaders opposed to segregation policies in Tredyffrin and Easttown schools.
“Many of us think of school segregation battles taking place in the deep south, but the fight for Civil Rights and equality in education extended into our area,” Comitta said. “It’s important that we continue to tell these stories, share their lessons, and preserve our historic places as part of American history. I want to thank the Rev. April M. Martin, pastor of Mt. Zion AME Church, and all the congregants and supporters working to preserve this historic site.”
“I am so very grateful to Senator Carolyn Comitta, who understood the urgent call to repair and restore Mt. Zion AME Historic Church in Devon. Its significant history has impacted both our Chester County and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania,” Martin said.
The church is well-known for its role in “the Berwyn School Fight,” which began in 1932 when school board leaders attempted to impose previously unenforced segregation policies in the districts’ schools. They planned to consolidate all black students, teachers and staff in two older schools, while the existing high school and a new elementary school would be reserved for white students. At that time, the decision was in line with the U.S. Supreme Court 1896
Plessy v. Ferguson
ruling that established the doctrine of “separate but equal.”
Since there were very few black-owned businesses and other friendly gathering places in the region, black families met at Mt. Zion AME Church to plan and strategize their protest efforts against the attempt at segregation. They signed a petition, enlisted the help of the NAACP, picketed the school, and even boycotted sending their children.
For a time, some children were taught in the church’s parsonage while others were homeschooled or traveled to nearby schools. Some did not attend school and their parents were threatened with losing their jobs, fined and even arrested and jailed for having “truant” children.
According to Roger Thorne of the Tredyffrin/Easttown Historical Society, who wrote
a detailed historical account of the case
, the jailings reportedly came to an end when a mother with an infant in her arms refused to pay the fine on principle and agreed to go to jail in place of her husband, so he would not lose his job. Her stand reportedly caused the court to stop arresting parents.
After two years of fighting and national attention on the case, Pennsylvania Attorney General Schnader intervened and in the spring of 1934, the segregation plan was scrapped, and black and white students returned to sharing the same classrooms.
The case had several impacts, including assisting in the passage of the Pennsylvania Equal Rights Bill in 1935, spurring on the organization and coalition-building efforts of the NAACP, and demonstrating the effectiveness of nonviolent resistance strategies and methods that would become the hallmark of the modern Civil Rights movement.
Still, it would be another two decades before the Supreme Court’s landmark
Brown v. Board of Education
ruling establishing segregation in public schools as unconstitutional.
Mt Zion AME Church is listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015, and in 2020, received a historic marker from the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission. Its cemetery is also the final resting place of numerous Civil War Veterans who served in the US Colored Troops (USCT).
Today, plans are in store to fully restore the church and develop an educational center on African American History there.

title: Comitta Secures Funding for Community Volunteers in Medicine

Comitta Secures Funding for Community Volunteers in Medicine
July 21, 2026
West Chester, Pa (July 22, 2026) –
Community Volunteers in Medicine (CVIM), a free clinic offering healthcare to uninsured working people and families with low incomes, was recently awarded state funding for important facility upgrades thanks to the work of state Senator Carolyn Comitta.
CVIM, which has served people in Chester County for nearly 30 years, is using the $50,000 grant to make infrastructure upgrades that strengthen the safety and security of patients, volunteers, and staff.
“Community Volunteers in Medicine is deeply grateful for this special grant, and for Senator Comitta’s commitment to our healthcare mission,” said CVIM President and CEO Karen Kofalt. “Your partnership is especially valuable as we prepare to serve even more community members losing health insurance and access to care.”
Comitta said she worked to secure the investment in CVIM at a time when more Pennsylvanians are losing health insurance coverage due to the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies and Medicaid cuts at the federal level.
“CVIM is a community asset and a lifeline for so many people in our community. As more working families are struggling with basic costs due to rising inflation, cuts to human services programs, and high insurance premiums, it’s vital that we continue to support and strengthen our healthcare infrastructure,” she said. “I’m thrilled to be able to help secure this investment, and I want to thank the healthcare heroes – doctors, nurses, and medical professionals – who volunteer their time at CVIM and other free clinics.”
One in three Pennsylvanians, including about 5,800 in Chester County, who bought a health plan through Pennie (the state’s ACA marketplace) last year have canceled their coverage. In addition, more than 300,000 Pennsylvanians are expected to become uninsured due to Medicaid changes and cuts at the federal level, according to the Shapiro administration.
CVIM has treated thousands of patients since its opening and last year cared for nearly 5,000 patients during 36,420 visits. The nonprofit organization offers primary and specialty medical care, comprehensive dental services, and free prescription medications to uninsured individuals and families earning less than 300% of the federal poverty level. Its operating budget is supported entirely by a generous community of philanthropic individuals, foundations, corporations, faith-based organizations, and civic groups.
For more information on CVIM, visit
cvim.org
.

awarded $200,000 for the demolition and renovation of the existing administrative office space, along with the construction of two new ADA-compliant additions.

is a Commonwealth grant program for the design, acquisition, and construction of regional economic, cultural, civic, recreational, and historical improvement projects.
